title: Three doors guarded (229–234)
hook: guard against anger of the body, of the tongue, of the mind
carry: the mind is where anger first knocks

segments.voice: Yesterday, akkodha: four harms, four opposite weapons, and Atula, who blamed everyone. Your line was overcome by giving. Today ends the week.

A house has three doors: a front door, a back door, and a side door by the garage. You can lock the front door every night, but if the side door is wide open, anyone can walk in. Anger is like a visitor who tries every door. Some of us guard our hands well: we'd never hit anyone. But the tongue is wide open. Or we're careful with words, and the mind is running a whole courtroom drama in the background. Chapter seventeen ends by checking every door in the house.
screen: `A HOUSE WITH THREE DOORS.` → `THE FRONT LOCKED, THE SIDE OPEN.` → `ANGER TRIES EVERY DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, a picture of a person nobody could honestly blame: like a coin of gold from the Jambu river, praised even by the gods. The way there: guard three doors. Verse two thirty-one, in Max Müller's translation: "Beware of bodily anger, and control thy body!" Verse two thirty-two: "Beware of the anger of the tongue, and control thy tongue!" And verse two thirty-three: "Beware of the anger of the mind, and control thy mind!" Each verse has two halves: stop the harm through that door, and use that same door for good. The body that could strike can also help. The tongue that could wound can also comfort. Then the chapter's last line, verse two thirty-four: "The wise who control their body, who control their tongue, the wise who control their mind, are indeed well controlled." Buddhist teaching calls these the three doors of action: body, speech and mind, in Pali kāya, vacī and mano. Every action, it says, goes out through one of them. That's why the ten classic wholesome actions are sorted this way: three for the body, four for speech, three for the mind. Notice which comes last. The mind is where anger first knocks, long before the tongue or the hand. Now look back at the week, a house with good doors. Health is the greatest gift. Keep good company. Love fully, hold loosely. Good deeds greet you. Other people are but holding the reins. Overcome by giving. And today: three doors guarded.
screen: `A COIN OF JAMBU-RIVER GOLD.` · `BODY, TONGUE, MIND.` · `STOP THE HARM; USE THE DOOR WELL.` · `THE MIND IS WHERE IT KNOCKS FIRST.` · then, large: `THREE DOORS GUARDED.`

segments.voice: Check each door in turn, the body first: notice your hands, your shoulders, your jaw, and let anything clenched soften. Then the tongue: if a sharp sentence is waiting behind your teeth, let it rest there, unspoken. Then the mind: if an argument is running in the background, notice it, and let it quiet down on the out-breath, three doors closed to anger and open to kindness.
Dvāra. A door, a gate: verses two thirty-one to two thirty-four say guard against anger of the body, of the tongue and of the mind, and use each for good.
Your line: the mind is where anger first knocks. Body, tongue, mind: one house, well kept. That closes the week.

howItsDone: Buddhist ethics sorts action into three doors, body, speech and mind, and the ten wholesome courses of action (three of body, four of speech, three of mind) are a common framework for daily reflection and confession.

fork.setup: you'd never hit anyone, and you're careful with words. but in your head you've been arguing with a coworker all morning. which door is open?
fork.reveal: verse 233: "beware of the anger of the mind, and control thy mind!" the mind is the door anger tries first.

original.note: Pali: a door or gate — the teaching of the three doors of action (kāya, vacī, mano) uses this word.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't lose your temper.
what it means: anger can come out through the body, the tongue or the mind, so guard all three, and use each door for good.
what a scholar hears: the kammadvāra, the three doors of action, organize the ten kusala kammapatha; the verses themselves name body, tongue and mind.
recall: a steady happiness and ease of mind
